title: One Ångström at the Rebounding Latch & Window Spark — Armstrong & Bezanilla’s 1973 Pronase Squid Axon, Raman & Bean’s Resurgent NaV1.6 Current, Tsien’s T-Type Window Current & Human SCN8A / CaV3.1 Cryo-EM (PDB 8FHD & 6KZP)

teenKit.tldr: Neurons aren't obedient textbook switches that rest quietly; they use hijacked molecular latches and atomic windows to fire at blinding speeds and sustain constant electrical sparks.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Without these sub-threshold sparks and rapid-fire molecular hacks, you couldn't coordinate a fast piano trroll, catch a falling glass, or even generate the rhythmic brain waves that keep you asleep.
keyTakeaways: High school textbook neurons that neatly fire a single spike and rest are a complete fiction compared to the high-performance reality of the central nervous system.
Classic experiments using internal pronase on squid giant axons proved that the sodium channel's fast inactivation is a physical swinging door or wedge.
Advanced cryo-EM imaging (like PDB 8FHD and 6KZP) lets scientists peer down to a single Ångström to see how channels handle ions and bind drugs like Z944.

vocab.meaning: The rapid electrical spike a neuron fires when it shoots up from rest to positive voltage.
The built-in molecular plug that slams a sodium channel shut milliseconds after it opens.
A persistent trickle of ions that leaks through channels when their opening and closing ranges overlap.
A high-tech imaging method that freezes biological molecules in liquid nitrogen to photograph their atomic structures.

quiz.question: What is the primary flaw of the standard textbook model of a neuron?
options: It assumes neurons never fire at all
It portrays neurons as overly tidy, single-spike switches when real high-performance circuits break that speed limit
It claims neurons run on water instead of electricity
It says neurons only function when a person is asleep
quiz.explanation: Real neurons in complex circuits pull off rapid-fire rebounding spikes and continuous background sparks that shatter the textbook speed limit.

quiz.question: What did Armstrong and Bezanilla discover in 1973 by injecting pronase into squid axons?
options: That sodium channels can be completely melted by hot water
That the inactivation off-switch is a physical piece that can be chopped away from the inside
That squids actually use calcium instead of sodium to think
That neurons communicate using radio waves
quiz.explanation: Pronase digests the internal molecular wedge responsible for fast inactivation, proving it is a physical plug rather than abstract math.

quiz.question: What do modern structural tools like PDB 8FHD and PDB 6KZP allow scientists to visualize?
options: The entire brain map of a living human while they sleep
The atomic layout of ion channels down to the single Ångström scale
The exact speed of sound traveling down a squid axon
How a neuron grows a new synapse from scratch
quiz.explanation: Cryo-EM structures like 8FHD and 6KZP zoom in to atomic resolution to reveal filters, wedges, and drug binding sites.
